catalog_locator: p. 3 (PDF page 3 of 5), section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)'; intonation remark p. 4, first paragraph
catalog_quote: Stress is phonemic. Its actual occurence cannot be predicted, though in a word of two syllables it most frequently occurs on the second syllable, and in a word of three syllables it generally occurs on the first or the third. Stress pairs: o:uwa [ˈouwɑ] 'grandfather' dui [du’i] 'go!' o:uwob [ouˈwob] 'butterfly' dui [’dui] 'listen!' [p. 4] Go:bosi is clearly an intonation language. While it is possible that words in isolation, or verb stems, have their own individual tone, it is clear that when these occur in a sentence with its own particular intonation pattern and sentence stress, the intonation pattern takes over and changes the tones that were recorded in isolation.

Page 4 opens verbatim with 'Go:bosi is c…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive and not predictable from the phonological shape of the word (minimal pairs dui 'go!' vs dui 'listen!'); statistically, disyllables are most often stressed on the second (final) syllable and trisyllables on the first or the third, i.e. a tendency to avoid the penult. The authors add that isolation-form tones/stress are overridden by sentence intonation and sentence stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated beyond the hedges 'most frequently' / 'generally'; the tendencies are explicitly not rules.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from words in isolation (citation forms). The OPD notes that in connected speech the sentence intonation pattern and sentence stress take over and change the pitch recorded in isolation. Draft SIL phonology data sheet (5 pp.), posted without peer review; the underlying analysis is Joan Rule's 1988 phoneme statement.
new_statements.identity_note: The source calls the language Go:bosi (Gobasi) [GOI], Western Province, East Strickland Family, population 1400; this is the same languoid as Glottolog goba1246 Gobasi (alt. Gebusi, Bibo, Nomad; dialects Oibae, Bibo, Honibo per Ethnologue/Wikipedia). The OPD does not name a dialect; Rule's data presumably come from the Nomad area SIL/mission contact. The first-language name 'Go:bosi' with long o corresponds to Knauft's 'Gebusi'.
